paras: The whipping of Buff Wright was an attack in the late summer of 1903 in Warsaw, Benton County, Missouri, in which a group of white townsmen took a young Black man from the town jail, whipped him, and ordered him to leave town. The case reached print mainly through the damage suit Wright brought against several of his attackers with the help of P. D. Hastain of Sedalia, which white papers in Missouri and Kansas reported and a Black Sedalia weekly championed.

Wright, called "Buff" Wright by the Butler Weekly Times and William Wright in a Sedalia wire dispatch, was being held in the Warsaw jail, or "calaboose," when the attack took place. By his own account, as given in the Butler paper, he was there on "a trivial charge made by his uncle"; none of the reports names the charge.

According to the wire dispatch, Wright was taken from the jail and whipped by "20 or more citizens." The Butler Weekly Times said he was "severely whipped" and ordered to leave town, while the Sedalia Times wrote that he had been driven out by white men of the town and bore "brutal scars on his head and body." The coverage gives no date for the whipping beyond placing it before September 1, when the dispatch was filed.

Wright went to Sedalia and retained Hastain, described in the dispatch as an ex-mayor, to sue his assailants for damages. The dispatch put the claim at $100,000, but the Butler Weekly Times, two weeks later, gave $25,000 and named the defendants as cattle buyers Charles Bibb and a man named Rice, harness dealer Harvey Bartlett, hardware merchant Joe Dice, and Sam Davis, a bookkeeper for the Osage Valley bank. The Sedalia Times reported that Hastain had spent several days in Warsaw on the case, believed he had a good case, and had "brought suit against a number of them who were in the affair." No report of arrests, criminal charges, or the outcome of the suit was found in the coverage.

Most white papers carried the story as a short Sedalia dispatch dated September 1 and headed "Missouri Negro Sues Whitecaps," which ran on September 4 in the Barton County Democrat and the Kinsley Graphic in Kansas and on September 5 in the Laclede Blade in Missouri. The dispatch built the item around the lawsuit and the size of the claim, calling Wright "a negro" and his attackers "citizens" in its text while its headline labeled them whitecaps. On September 17 the Butler Weekly Times ran a longer paragraph among its local notes, naming the defendants and their trades and reporting without comment Wright's claim that there was "no excuse" for the whipping.

The only Black-press coverage found, in the Sedalia Times of September 12, took Wright's side openly, calling him "a poor helpless Negro boy" who had been "shamefully whipped" by "a gang of lawless" white men "without any cause whatever." The paper praised Hastain as "a friend to the Negro" and quoted his promise that he would "learn somebody a lesson on whipping Negroes in Benton county." Where the white reports confined themselves to the jail, the whipping and the suit, the Sedalia weekly cast the whipping as unprovoked and the suit as a lesson to the white men of Benton County.

The reports differ on the damages sought, $100,000 in the wire and $25,000 in the Butler paper, which was later and named the defendants, though neither explains the gap. They also differ on Wright's age, the Sedalia Times calling him a "colored boy" and the Butler paper "a young negro man."
